reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Cranes, Rigs, Leads, Templates, Helmets, and Cushions
sections.summary: Primary driving system components: crane (crawler preferred for mobility/stability; truck/rough-terrain cranes also used), leads (swinging most common — lightweight and flexible; fixed and semi-fixed leads provide better alignment), helmets (0.1-0.2 inch clearance over pile; two-piece with insert for multiple pile types), hammer cushions (proprietary man-made polymers; no hardwood, wire rope, asbestos, or highly elastic materials), pile cushions (plywood for concrete piles only — replaceable per ~1,500 blows). Templates required for offshore/swinging leads when pile head is below water or excavation.
sections.body:
Cranes (Section 15.1): Crawler cranes are most common — good mobility, wide base stability, 360-degree hoisting radius. Must be trucked to site and assembled. Firm ground or crane mats required. Truck (mobile) cranes have good mobility but cannot walk with loads; outriggers used for stability. Rough terrain cranes set up quickly and have greater mobility in difficult terrain; restricted side lifting.

Dedicated and Universal Rigs (Section 15.2): Specialty rigs with attached telescoping leaders that transition hydraulically from transport to vertical driving position — fast setup without additional heavy equipment. Winch lines for pile offloading and lofting.

Leads (Section 15.3): Maintain hammer-pile alignment for concentric blows. Types: swinging (most common — lightweight, low cost, flexible placement, largest crane radius), fixed, semi-fixed/vertical travel, and offshore. Stabbing guide at bottom of swinging leads aligns pile into leads. Offshore leads with templates used over water.

Templates (Section 15.4): Required to hold piles in position over water or excavations. Template top should be within 5 feet of cutoff elevation or water elevation, whichever is lower. Template batter pile locations must account for offset from template elevation to cutoff elevation (1H:4V batter = 15-inch offset per 5 feet of template height). Rollers preferred in templates, particularly for batter piles.

Helmets (Section 15.5): Protect pile head during driving. Helmet or insert should fit loosely but maintain alignment — 0.1 to 0.2 inches larger than pile diameter. One-piece helmets manufactured for specific pile types; two-piece (base + insert) accommodates multiple pile types and sizes. Proper alignment is critical for precast concrete piles.

Hammer Cushions (Section 15.6): Absorb impact shock to protect hammer. Proprietary man-made materials (micarta, nylon, urethane, durable polymers). Cushion materials become compressed and stiffen with use — may require replacement. Proprietary cushions last up to 200 hours of driving. Prohibited materials: hardwood, small pieces of wood, wire rope, highly elastic materials, asbestos-containing materials.

Pile Cushions (Section 15.7): Required for concrete piles between helmet and pile head to prevent concrete pile damage. Typically plywood. Pile cushions deteriorate faster than hammer cushions. Should be replaced after approximately 1,500 hammer blows. New cushions change wave equation results and should not be replaced just before end of driving.
key_points: Crawler cranes most common for pile driving; require crane mats in soft ground; 360-degree hoisting radius
Swinging leads: most common — lightweight, flexible, largest crane radius; stabbing guide for pile alignment
Template: top within 5 ft of cutoff or water elevation; account for batter pile offset at template elevation
Helmet clearance: 0.1-0.2 inches over pile diameter; two-piece (base + insert) for multiple pile types
Hammer cushion: proprietary polymers (micarta, nylon, urethane); lasts up to 200 hrs; no hardwood/wire rope/asbestos
Pile cushion (concrete piles): plywood; replace after ~1,500 blows; avoid replacement just before end of driving
Vibratory hammers do not require leads; hydraulic clamp connects directly to pile head
sections.applicability: Description and selection guidance for crane types, lead systems, templates, helmets, hammer cushions, and pile cushions in driven pile installation.

sections.title: Impact Hammer Types
sections.summary: Impact hammers classified as: single-acting air/steam (7-1,800 ft-kips; 35-60 blows/min; versatile for all piles especially large concrete/pipe), double-acting air/steam (1-21 ft-kips; 95-300 blows/min; lighter, more productive), differential air/steam (15-50 ft-kips; less air volume than double-acting), open-end (single-acting) diesel (9-1,620 ft-kips; 40-60 blows/min; most common; stroke varies with resistance), closed-end (double-acting) diesel (5-73 ft-kips; 80-105 blows/min), single-acting hydraulic (25-2,162 ft-kips; 30-50 blows/min; variable energy), double-acting hydraulic (25-2,581 ft-kips; 40-90 blows/min; widest energy range). Table 15-1 provides full hammer characteristics.
sections.body:
Table 15-1 presents characteristics and uses of all hammer types. Detailed descriptions follow:

Drop Hammers (Section 15.9): 7-60 ft-kips; 4-8 blows/min; 23-33 ft/sec impact velocity. Lowest initial cost. Simple to operate. Not for concrete piles. Limited to Rn ≤ 120 kips unless wave equation approval obtained. Ram weight minimum 2.0 kips. Drop height maximum 12 ft. Ram weight ≥ helmet + pile weight. Requires hammer guides for concentric impact.

Single-Acting Air/Steam Hammers (Section 15.10): 7-1,800 ft-kips; 35-60 blows/min. Ram lifted by air/steam pressure and falls under gravity (single-acting). Versatile for any pile type, particularly large concrete and steel pipe piles. Requires external air compressor or steam plant. Energy = ram weight × stroke. Striking parts weight ≥ 1/3 of helmet + pile weight; ≥ 2.75 kips.

Double-Acting Air/Steam Hammers (Section 15.11): 1-21 ft-kips; 95-300 blows/min. Ram accelerates downward under air/steam pressure in addition to gravity. More productive than single-acting. Some models fully enclosed for underwater driving. Energy = (ram weight + effective piston area × fluid pressure) × stroke.

Differential Acting Air/Steam Hammers (Section 15.12): 15-50 ft-kips; 98-300 blows/min. Similar to double-acting but uses less air/steam volume. Lower impact velocity than double-acting.

Single-Acting (Open-End) Diesel Hammers (Section 15.13): 9-1,620 ft-kips; 40-60 blows/min. Most commonly used hammer type. Combustion gas from diesel ignition lifts the ram. Stroke varies with pile resistance — greater resistance produces higher strokes. Variable stroke a useful field indicator. Requires visible stroke measurement device (rings on ram); contractor provides stroke-to-blows/min chart; automatic stroke display device required.

Double-Acting (Closed-End) Diesel Hammers (Section 15.14): 5-73 ft-kips; 80-105 blows/min. Combustion in both directions. Bounce chamber pressure measured to determine energy. Contractor provides bounce chamber pressure-to-energy/stroke chart calibrated within 60 days.

Single-Acting Hydraulic Hammers (Section 15.15): 25-2,162 ft-kips; 30-50 blows/min. Fully variable energy over wide range. Suitable for all pile types. More complex than air/steam hammers. Kinetic energy or ram impact velocity automatically displayed.

Double-Acting Hydraulic Hammers (Section 15.16): 25-2,581 ft-kips; 40-90 blows/min. Widest rated energy range of all hammer types. Energy variable in both up and down ram travel.
key_points: Most common: open-end single-acting diesel (9-1,620 ft-kips; 40-60 bpm); stroke varies with resistance
Single-acting air/steam (7-1,800 ft-kips): versatile for large concrete/pipe; requires external compressor
Double-acting air/steam (1-21 ft-kips): most productive at 95-300 bpm; some models underwater-capable
Drop hammers: Rn ≤ 120 kips; ram ≥ 2.0 kips; drop ≤ 12 ft; NOT for concrete piles
Hydraulic hammers: fully variable energy; kinetic energy or impact velocity displayed automatically
Open-end diesel: automatic stroke display device required; bounce chamber gauge not applicable
Closed-end diesel: bounce chamber pressure gauge and calibrated chart required within 60 days
Table 15-1: full comparison of hammer types — rated energy, blow rate, impact velocity, pile suitability

tables.description: Typical pile hammer characteristics and uses — rated energy (ft-kips), impact velocity (ft/sec), blow rate (blows/min), energy formula, lifting power, maintenance, pile suitability, advantages, disadvantages, and remarks for all hammer types (single/double-acting air/steam, differential, single/double-acting diesel, drop, single/double-acting hydraulic, vibratory, resonant)

sections.applicability: Description, energy ranges, operating characteristics, and application guidance for all driven pile hammer types used in practice.

sections.title: Vibratory and Resonant Hammers
sections.summary: Vibratory hammers use paired counter-rotating eccentric weights to produce sinusoidal axial force (750-2,400 vibrations/min). Most effective in granular soils; less effective in stiff-to-hard clays. Do not require leads. Suitable for H-piles, open-end pipes, sheet piles; not for precast concrete. No reliable method for nominal resistance estimation during vibratory installation — resistance must be confirmed by restrike with impact hammer. Variable moment vibratory hammers can be brought to full speed without eccentric moment, avoiding critical vibration frequencies.
sections.body:
Vibratory Hammers (Section 15.17): Paired counter-rotating eccentric weights produce a sinusoidal axial force at 750-2,400 vibrations per minute (standard up to 1,600 RPM/26 Hz; variable moment up to 2,300-2,400 RPM/40 Hz; low frequency up to 1,200 RPM/20 Hz). Horizontal force components cancel; only vertical remains. Hydraulic clamp rigidly connects hammer to pile head. No leads required; templates used for sheet pile cells.

Vibratory hammers are most effective in granular soils, particularly when submerged. Also effective in silty or softer clays; less effective in stiff-to-hard clays. Suitable for: sheet piles, H-piles, and open-end pipe piles (non-displacement types). Not suitable for precast concrete piles due to tensile and bending stress concerns. Difficult for closed-end pipes and other displacement piles.

Variable moment hammers can ramp up to operating speed with eccentric weights in neutral (no force), avoiding resonance with natural frequencies of nearby structures. Most important for startup and shutdown, which produce the greatest vibration effects.

No reliable nominal resistance estimation method during vibratory installation. Must confirm resistance by impact hammer restrike after installation. Some wave equation programs simulate vibratory driving and dynamic measurements have been made, but no validated approach exists.

Resonant Hammers (Section 15.18): Operate at very high vibration frequencies (up to 10,800 vibrations/minute). Designed to achieve resonance with the pile to maximize energy transmission. Limited commercial availability and use in practice.
key_points: Vibratory hammers: 750-2,400 vpm; paired counter-rotating eccentric weights; horizontal components cancel
Most effective in granular soils (especially submerged); less effective in stiff-to-hard clays
Not for precast concrete piles (tensile/bending damage); suitable for H-piles, open-end pipe, sheet piles
No reliable nominal resistance estimation during vibratory driving — restrike with impact hammer required
Variable moment hammers: ramp to operating speed with eccentric moment neutral to avoid critical resonant frequencies
Startup/shutdown produce greatest vibration concerns for nearby structures
Resonant hammers: up to 10,800 vpm; very limited availability and use in practice
sections.applicability: Vibratory hammer operating characteristics, soil suitability, limitations for resistance estimation, and guidance on variable moment hammers to control construction vibrations.

sections.title: Hammer Size Selection, Energy Monitoring, and Noise Suppression
sections.summary: Preliminary hammer size: ram weight 1-2% of nominal/driving resistance; Table 15-2 minimum rated energies (12,000-42,000 ft-lbs by Rn range). Wave equation analysis is the recommended selection method — dynamic formula approach not recommended. Kinetic energy monitoring devices (proximity switches, E-Saximeter) provide real-time ram velocity, energy, stroke, and blow rate. Impact driving noise: 80-130 dBa; optional manufacturer noise shrouds reduce by ~10 dBa. Underwater noise suppression: bubble curtain systems effective for marine environments.
sections.body:
Impact Hammer Size Selection (Section 15.19): Use of dynamic pile formulas for hammer energy and size selection is not recommended — they assume desired nominal resistance is achieved and become increasingly inaccurate as hammer complexity and required Rn increase. Wave equation analysis is the recommended selection method.

Preliminary sizing rule: ram weight = 1 to 2% of required nominal resistance or nominal driving resistance (whichever is greater) as a first estimate. Table 15-2 provides minimum manufacturer-rated energy by Rn range: Rn ≤ 180 kips: 12,000 ft-lbs; 181-300 kips: 21,000 ft-lbs; 301-415 kips: 28,800 ft-lbs; 416-540 kips: 37,600 ft-lbs; 541-600 kips: 42,000 ft-lbs. These are generalizations — modify for pile type, load, length, and local soils. For short piles to rock, smaller hammer may be more appropriate for stress control. Table 15-2 should not be used directly in a specification.

Hammer Kinetic Energy Monitoring (Section 15.20): Several hammers available with built-in kinetic energy readout from factory proximity switches. Measures: impact velocity, kinetic energy, blow rate, and (for single-acting diesel) hammer stroke. Existing hammers can be retrofitted with proximity switches (1.2-inch bore drill holes above combustion chamber for diesel hammers). Wireless E-Saximeter receives transmitter signal; can also function as a driving log. Particularly valuable on large projects or high-resistance piles to detect performance changes requiring criterion adjustment.

Noise Suppression (Section 15.21): Impact pile driving: 80-130 dBa depending on hammer and pile type. Local ordinances may limit noise levels. Manufacturer noise shrouds available for some diesel and hydraulic hammers — reduce noise by approximately 10 dBa.

Underwater Noise Suppression (Section 15.22): Bubble curtain systems inject air through perforated hoses around the pile to create an air bubble barrier that attenuates underwater acoustic energy. Effective for protecting marine life in environmentally sensitive areas. Reinhall et al. (2014) evaluated acoustic shield approach for further attenuation.
key_points: Preliminary hammer size: ram weight = 1-2% of required Rn or Rndr (whichever greater)
Table 15-2 minimum rated energy: 12,000 ft-lbs (Rn≤180 kips), 21,000 (181-300), 28,800 (301-415), 37,600 (416-540), 42,000 (541-600) — for preliminary screening only, not for specifications
Wave equation analysis is the recommended hammer selection method; dynamic formula not recommended
Kinetic energy monitoring: proximity switches measure impact velocity, energy, stroke; wireless E-Saximeter readout
Retrofittable on any hammer (1.2-inch bore holes in diesel cylinder above combustion chamber)
Impact driving noise: 80-130 dBa; manufacturer shrouds reduce by ~10 dBa
Bubble curtain systems: perforated hoses around pile inject air; protect marine life from underwater acoustic energy

tables.description: Preliminary hammer energy requirements by nominal resistance — minimum manufacturer's rated energy (ft-lbs) for Rn ranges: ≤180 kips: 12,000; 181-300: 21,000; 301-415: 28,800; 416-540: 37,600; 541-600: 42,000; for preliminary equipment evaluation only, not for use in specifications

sections.applicability: Hammer size selection criteria, kinetic energy monitoring devices, and noise suppression equipment for driven pile projects, including preliminary energy estimates from Table 15-2.

sections.title: Followers, Jetting, Predrilling, Spudding, and Equipment Submittals
sections.summary: Followers transmit hammer blows below lead reach; follower stiffness should match equivalent pile length; energy losses estimated by wave equation or dynamic measurements. Jetting displaces soil with water/air — limited to end-bearing piles (not friction piles); final resistance must be obtained by impact driving; rarely used due to environmental restrictions. Predrilling for obstructions, embankments, or vibration reduction; diameter 4 inches less than pile diagonal (H-pile/square) or 1 inch less than pile diameter (round). Spudding opens hole in dense fill or debris without bringing cuttings to surface.
sections.body:
Followers (Section 15.23): A follower is a structural member between hammer and pile head when pile head is below lead reach (below deck, underwater, or below grade). Maintains pile alignment is difficult for batter piles using followers. Energy loss in follower and connection reduces effective blow energy transmitted to pile — estimated by wave equation or dynamic measurements. Properly designed follower: stiffness (per unit length) approximately equal to equivalent pile length stiffness. Followers with significantly less stiffness should be avoided. Consider underwater-rated hammers as an alternative.

Jetting (Section 15.24): High-pressure water (or air + water) displaces soil to facilitate pile penetration. Jets may be inside or outside the pile. Most effective in loose-to-medium dense granular soils. Not recommended for friction piles (reduces frictional resistance). Should be avoided for laterally loaded piles. For end-bearing piles: final resistance must be obtained by driving (no jetting). Backfill open jetted holes after installation. Jetting greatly reduced due to environmental restrictions on disposal of jetted material and groundwater.

Predrilling (Section 15.25): Soil augers or rotary drills used to: (1) penetrate obstructions (old timbers, boulders, riprap); (2) install piles through compacted embankments; (3) reduce heave from closely spaced displacement piles. Hole diameter guidance: 4 inches less than diagonal of square or H-piles; 1 inch less than diameter for round piles. Through very hard material: diameter may equal pile diagonal/diameter. In embankments: up to 6 inches larger than greatest pile dimension. Pile is driven with impact hammer after placement in predrilled hole.

Spudding (Section 15.26): Short, strong member driven or dropped through dense fill/debris, then removed. Alternative to jetting or predrilling in miscellaneous fill/debris. Does not bring cuttings or groundwater to surface (environmental advantage). Risk: spud may not be removable if driven too deep. Requires written engineer approval per specification.

Equipment Submittals (Section 15.27): Contractor submits all proposed equipment details and procedures prior to driving. Engineer uses submittal to perform wave equation analysis and provide preliminary/final driving criteria. Drive system submittal form (Figure 15-50): hammer components and accessories, pile type/section/splicing/toe details, plus jetting/predrilling/spudding equipment details as applicable.
key_points: Follower stiffness should match equivalent length of pile — significantly softer followers not acceptable
Follower energy losses estimated by wave equation analysis or dynamic measurements; avoid when possible
Jetting: not for friction piles or laterally loaded piles; final resistance must come from impact driving; rarely used due to environmental restrictions
Predrilling: 4 inches less than pile diagonal (H-pile/square) or 1 inch less than pile diameter (round); up to 6 inches larger than pile in embankments
Predrilling stops ≥5 ft above plan pile toe elevation for non-end-bearing; may go to rock for end-bearing
Spudding: no cuttings to surface (environmental advantage); spud may become unremovable if driven too deep
Equipment submittal with wave equation analysis required before driving — provides basis for driving criterion
sections.applicability: Guidance on followers, jetting, predrilling, and spudding installation aids for driven piles; equipment submittal requirements and their role in developing wave equation-based driving criteria.
